I asked my dad about sex when I was five, and he briefly explained:: “Sex is what you do when you are older and you find a friend you want to have children with.” It was a good tip, but it left out the whole question of romance: why that friend rather than one of the others, what problems people have in relationships, and how to prevent or handle them. I can’t expect my dad to have developed a whole guide to all that, because that wasn’t his main mission. So I ended up learning most of it the hard way, and this is what I’d like to pass on to my kids, although by the time they read it, the existence of natural humans, romance, and love might be long forgotten, for all I know. This guide isn’t universally applicable for everyone even now, since it comes from my particular life experience (including influences I’ve had from friends & research). I’m a straight man, and I’m writing from relationships I’ve had with women, so she and her are going to show up a lot. Most of this has nothing specifically to do with being male or straight. The Primal Attraction section is the exception, because there I’m specifically talking about the man-woman dynamic I’ve actually lived.
What we mean by “love” ❤️
English isn’t a scientific language when it comes to love. This leads to a lot of romantic confusion because we don’t have one word for one meaning.

One meaning is selfless love—what contemplative traditions call agape, metta, loving-kindness, divine love, and so forth. In Buddhist metta practice you sit there wishing, “May all beings be at ease, pure of heart, and free.” It’s not about them being yours.

Then we use the same word for romantic love (eros): I want you. I want your attention and your body. I want to be special to you, and I want our lives tangled up together. I don’t think there’s anything fake or shameful about this.
A good relationship must have both kinds of love at once. Too often, the trouble is there’s a whole lot of I want you and hardly any I want you to be happy.

Most people fail this test: what would I want if she herself thought she’d be happier with somebody else? But if they can get past the initial horror, the conflict starts to fall apart. Being wanted is part of what makes me want someone.

But the horror is unavoidable, because I can’t wait until I know I’m wanted before I let her know I want her. If we both do that, nothing gets started. And it doesn’t stop being true once we’re together. If I start feeling less wanted, I may pull back. She feels me pulling back and starts feeling less wanted herself, then she pulls back too.

Agape or divine love does two jobs at once to rescue erotic love. First, most obviously, it keeps eros from becoming totally selfish and fickle by making the other person’s happiness part of the wanting: I want you because I know you’ll be happy with me. Second, it gives eros a landing pad. When two people pull away because eros seems unreciprocated for a moment, the backdrop of actual, genuine care, keeps the couple from simply abandoning each other, and then they might even rekindle the eros when they see that it’s based on something deeper.
Eros can help build the agape too. It has a drive to it: it keeps pulling me toward this particular person, and over time that closeness can grow an agape that survives the drive itself.

That drive can weaken for reasons that aren’t really my fault. I can get old, sick, depressed, or grieving, and I would hope the agape is deep enough that she sticks by me through some of that even if it puts strain on eros. But if I just get bored with life, stop having much of a life outside her, and make her responsible for nearly all my warmth, meaning, reassurance, and excitement, that’s different. I don’t get to be shocked if she wants me less.
Talk about making love before you do it

From here on, when I say making love, I’m talking about two people who care about each other deeply and feel super connected, using their bodies as part of that connection. If you’ve never experienced this, it may be like trying to explain the taste of an orange. If you don’t know what love is, you don’t know. That’s another conversation, and I’d suggest reading my inner child reparenting guide.
Having sex is just the physical act, whether that deeper connection is there or not. But sometimes it can create the connection also.

What I eventually took from my dad’s advice was a bigger question: would we like to raise children together? Are we ready? If we can really talk about raising children together, most of the other important questions come up on their own. What kind of life do I want? What kind of life do you want? What would we want for a child? What would sex mean between us?

What do you actually want? You may know some of it and not the rest. What makes your body relax and open? Is there anything kinky you need to be able to say out loud? What has your past made you want, or made you avoid? What just doesn’t work?
You may not know all the answers yet. “I don’t know, but I’m willing to find out honestly with you” is a perfectly good answer.

And what is sex for each of you? One person may mainly think of bonding while the other thinks of play. Sometimes it may feel sacred; another time it may just be how you come down from a bad day. It doesn’t have to mean the same thing every time.

It’s important to talk about sexual compatibility before getting undressed, even if that kills the vibe. Or even especially if it does kill the vibe, actually, since that’s a red flag if talking ruins things. And this applies whether you’re leaning too libertine or too traditional. And once you are undressed, the communication doesn’t stop there either. Can you feel comfortable with each other enough to express what turns you on, what this means to you, and what you’re unsure about? It’s that psychological trust & intimacy that builds the bridge between “having sex” and “making love.”

I remember reading a Christian magazine’s letter from a newlywed Christian woman who found out that her husband didn’t have much interest in sex after she saved herself for marriage. He trapped her, because he knew she would not feel good about divorce due to the religion. Of course, it didn’t have to be nefarious. I had a relationship with E. that was a bit like that about 15yrs ago. She wanted sex once a week, and it was driving me nuts because my libido was thru the roof. She also had no interest in trying to take a safe herb or supplement to increase her desire. Of course everyone does change over time as well. If our libidos later diverge, it’s better to talk about what we’d do before either person is already hurt.
Affection and the simmer

Doug Toft, who has been married for fifty years, has a useful list called 50 Things I Learned from 50 Years of Marriage. One of his points is to touch his wife without an agenda. A hug, cuddle, kiss, or back rub should sometimes be allowed to end right there. If every affectionate touch becomes a bid for sex, affection itself can start feeling like pressure.

text: Kim Anami calls the sexual current between encounters “the simmer”. Maybe she texts from work, “I can’t wait to touch you.” Maybe he tells her what he wants to do later. If we supposedly want each other but hardly ever flirt or let each other know it, that’s called taking each other for granted. Great sex probably isn’t going to materialize out of nowhere at bedtime just based on the flirting you did 5 years ago.
It shouldn’t become relationship homework, either: “Hey babe, Kim Anami told me to flirt with you more.”

And if our sex life suddenly changes, keep some curiosity about why rather than automatically going with the flow and creating a potential “new normal.” Maybe we’re pissed off at each other. Maybe one of us doesn’t feel wanted. Maybe somebody’s sick, stressed, on a new medication, whatever.

I also don’t want my partner to have to manufacture my desire for me. And if sex is one of the main things separating our relationship from friendship, giving it whatever exhausted scraps are left after everything else seems pretty dumb.
Can Casual Sex or a Situationship Actually Be Honest?

Your body doesn’t know that you picked someone up at a bar and agreed it was only for fun. Then the next morning, you’re wondering why they didn’t call. Well, not getting pulled in any further is the best outcome still available, actually, since you just played Russian Roulette with a potential life bond to a stranger.
“I don’t know whether I want something serious with you. I’m not pretending I do. I’d still like to have sex.”

That may be candid about what you expect now. It doesn’t settle what either of you will owe if the act creates something neither of you expected. Sex can make a child. If this girl gets pregnant, she’s gonna call you. Then what? You block her? Agree to child support? Try to convince her to abort if she thinks abortion is killing her child? Or vice versa. My first girlfriend, a diehard Baptist, aborted and told me a year later, because she “didn’t want to trap” me. This is what penetrative sex can do. No contraception is perfect.
The STI part is easy: say what you know, or say you don’t know. Feelings aren’t as easy, unless you’re both really numb or robotic about sex.
You have to care what happens to the person afterward. Otherwise you’re using and abusing them for pleasure. Maybe they’re using you too. Congratulations, now it’s mutual.

A lot of “I only want fun” really means, “This is the only version of the relationship that gets me laid.” Sometimes I know I’m hoping it turns into love. Sometimes I only find out I was hoping that when it doesn’t.
Situationships

And then there’s the situationship, which is hard to define because that’s basically the point. Usually it’s a happenstance relationship based on sex. There’s less communication, and what communication exists is more superficial. Yet it is obviously some kind of relationship even while one or both people refuse to name it. You’re regularly having sex, going out together, spending time alone together, and doing things you wouldn’t do with a regular friend. It feels like it’s filling a relationship void, but only accidentally and occasionally—maybe just enough to keep you from looking for anything deeper.

It can go either way. Often the man wants to keep it undefined while the woman wants commitment, partly because she’s the one risking pregnancy. Whoever keeps it undefined gets the fun without the responsibility. Refusing to name the relationship doesn’t make the responsibility disappear. What they don’t escape is the existential void created by another superficial fix. Doomscrolling entertains you too.

And “Why are you making this heavy?” can be a real question. They may actually mean: don’t you want the fun, and are you about to give it up? My answer would be: I’m trying to understand whether this is really fulfilling me or if it’s drainingly superficial.

I had something sort of like that with H., although ours was much deeper than what people normally mean by situationship. We were (and still are) BFFs, and spent nearly all our time together. She was falling in love with me, and I wasn’t falling in love with her. She felt more like a sister to me, partly because I’m not attracted to white women. Ours wasn’t superficial. It was just painfully uneven.
Labels Are Descriptive, Not Prescriptive
Here’s the funny thing many people don’t understand: labels don’t create commitment. They can still expose whether two people think they’re in the same relationship, which matters a lot.

True commitment grows out of relational depth, not a label. If we spend hours telling each other our deepest longings, fears, and problems, I’ll naturally be ready to help when you need me. I don’t need to promise that on paper. If someone says “I love you, I feel you, I’m here for you,” yet they hardly ever talk to you about what matters, that’s a red flag.

The person getting more of what they want may think the arrangement is fulfilling. Usually they’re just less aware that it isn’t. In college I had a friend with four girlfriends who boasted about it to girls while trying to get a fifth. I asked him, “But are you really happy?” He said, “No, I’m miserable, dude. I feel empty inside.”

The full conversation is so big that almost nobody would have casual sex if they took it seriously. Which is why almost nobody has the full conversation. I can’t decide what is okay for anybody else. I can say that most people who defend casual sex are not being very honest with themselves about pregnancy, attachment, or what they might owe the person afterward.

Outside a loving poly community or tribe, I think honest casual sex is almost impossible. If you want something closer to “casual love-making” without quite so many ways to damage each other, you probably need to find a free-love community where the people aren’t disposable, the bonds can be acknowledged, and any children have a village. But if the community is specifically designed to prioritize free love, you might find it attracts people who have traumas that produce trouble with connecting deeply, as ex-Tamera leader, Martin Winiecki wrote about after leaving recently.
Should you be in a relationship at all?

This is a horrible catch-22. Wounded people get lonely, and loneliness itself can kill. But the wounds that make somebody desperate for a relationship may also make them a terrible person to be in one with. People don’t only trigger each other and learn lessons. Sometimes they terrorize or kill each other.

I’m pretty conservative about this. I would tell most of my friends not to date yet. First love your inner child. If you can’t even do that, forget a relationship for now. Get a cat or a puppy. If you’re dishonest, can’t care what happens to another person, or keep turning every relationship into the same disaster, come on. You’re not ready.

You don’t have to be completely healed, but the present-day adult has to be able to parent whatever intimacy wakes up inside you, and responsible enough to deal with an actual child if sex creates one. If you can’t be a parent in either sense, you aren’t ready to date.

A good relationship can teach you self-love too, which is part of the problem: you may need one most when you’re least capable of creating a good one, recognizing one, or keeping it good. It depends what each of you are ready for and have the resources for. Here’s a video that can help understand the long process.

text: I wasn’t ready, but I was lucky

At twenty, I thought I was totally fine until I became enamored with Alba. She was Dominican, and warm in a way I didn’t understand. Kissing your BFF on the lips was normal to her. I thought she was in love with me. She did love me and wanted me living with her, but not in the way I wanted. The confusion threw me into a horrible spell for years. I was even a bit suicidal while living with her.

Then Bee cracked me open. My second wife and I were about as in love as two people could be, considering that every other day she would demonize me because of BPD. Before Bee, I didn’t know what In Love meant. Nobody knows until it happens. It’s a completely different kind of reality. It’s spiritual.

Did it heal her? We still can’t understand. During our two years together, it seemed to stabilize and heal some things while provoking her demons even more. Did it heal me? The relationship almost killed me, but I would never undo it. I still love her so much. I haven’t spoken with her in a year, but I love sending her love.

Relationships ALWAYS reveal what I can’t see. My selfishness. The depth that is actually available versus the depth I idealize. The other person’s selfishness and dishonesty and superficiality. How deeply I really love. How deep my illusions go. Whether my spirituality survives contact with another human being. Everything.
Spirituality to bypass intimacy

I’ve used spirituality as a replacement for intimacy a lot because intimacy was simply unavailable. As a boy and young man, I was so deprived of female touch that it was driving me insane. Meditation sometimes helped me cope better with the deprivation, but it wasn’t a cure. I remember once as I was entering into an ayahuasca ego death, I said, “Actually, I really just want a girlfriend.” Right then, the crazy trip abruptly ended, and a voice said, “Ok then go find one.” Nobody believes this story when I tell it.

I don’t believe most people can be truly happy celibate. People generally aren’t so serious about spiritual liberation that giving up sex and partnership for life makes sense. The Buddha didn’t advise everyone to become monastics.
If becoming a monastic genuinely makes you happier and more peaceful, stay. It might work for some very advanced people, or if your sexual desire is already low, or you’re old, etc.

But how do you know what you’re not aware of? Inner-child reparenting and self-hypnosis can help a lot with that, because often the inner child is being ignored while the adult is feeling some kind of liberation.

And if you’re so happy and free, what happens when you’re alone in a room with a super beautiful girl and she wants you? Or vice versa for women. Do you feel like you’re losing some control? Are you afraid?

Bhante Gunaratana, a famous Buddhist teacher, tells a story like this in his autobiography. A super beautiful girl at a retreat he was teaching snuck into his room and waited for him in bed, naked. He went nuts and started screaming at her “Get out!” at the top of his lungs. Obviously he was still repressing something, and she was adept at unintentionally uncovering it.

Robes do nothing. I was mildly molested in public by the abbot of one of Thailand’s largest Buddhist retreat centers. In Thailand, parents have very good reasons not to leave children alone with monks. Tibet is worse.

text: Forced celibacy doesn’t abolish anyone’s sexuality. For most people it eventually sends it somewhere weird. Why wouldn’t it?

There are practical reasons to become a monastic too. In a poor country it can mean free food, a place to live, status, and escape from ordinary responsibilities. In the West, the free food may matter less, but a person who received no particular respect as a layman can become Venerable Somebody and suddenly people bow to him.
Of course, he may sincerely want liberation, too. People can want several things at once.
Practical partnerships

I’ve traveled the world as a (white) guy from a first-world country. Many women have wanted to marry me partly because they figured I could improve their status and comfort. That always makes me feel sad and lonely to think about, but yeah, I know it’s to be expected. The funniest time was when a female police officer in India said we should marry because we were both the same age. 😜

It’s reasonable for a woman to want support, since after all, she has to provide for her potential children, but it muddies the waters for me. I’m not stupid; I understand that she might really love me while still wanting money, stability, children, a visa, a home, etc. Men aren’t a different species, although sometimes I think I might be. A man can really love a woman for who she is while also seeing her as a source of sex, children, social legitimacy, or help running the house. Affection and practical motives often coexist, even if it isn’t the romantic ideal.

And hey, sometimes being objectified is kinda sexy, too. Men like to be objectified to a certain degree as providers and defenders, just as women often like being seen as sex dolls by the men they want. Being wanted that way feels good, but feeling held is important as well.

But I don’t want to be just a provider-and-defender machine, because that’s vulnerable to hypergamy. I wanna know that if I fall ill or lose my job, I can count on my wife still. Guys want a ride-or-die chick. A woman also wants to know that when she gets old, sick, or no longer looks like the fantasy that first attracted her man, he will still happily stay.
It always goes deeper

And the question is more than just a practical one. It’s philosophical. Men have this (often subconscious) insecurity inside the provider role: how much does she love me, and how much does she love what I can do for her?

I don’t need the answer to be that provision had nothing to do with attraction. Being competent, protective, useful, and able to make things happen may be part of what draws a woman to a man, just as her beauty and sexuality may be part of what draws him to her. I want the bond to become bigger than the qualities that first made us desirable. Because as Bee always said, “You’re either going up, or going down.”

I had wondered for years how much a woman would love me if I couldn’t really provide for her. Then Bee told me, “I would rather be with you in the forest than with any other man in a mansion.” That’s what made me fall in love with her.

I got a smaller and much less romantic test later. Bee gave me some shoes to try that didn’t fit. I wore them for a day, and somehow my knee ended up messed up for about a month. She did nurse me, but a bit reluctantly. She also kept pushing me toward thinking maybe it was partly in my head or wasn’t really that bad. I understood why—neither of us could believe one day in the wrong shoes could do that—but it still felt dismissive, and maybe partly reflected what she wanted to be true.

Before me, Bee had also stayed with a boyfriend who was totally broke and crazy and supported him for a while. Later she blamed herself for staying through that, and I agree. Helping carry somebody through temporary incapacity is different from becoming the permanent support system for a man who won’t take responsibility. Some women are fixer types, which can create the opposite pattern.
What makes me desirable is not the same question as what makes me loved when I temporarily stop being desirable in that particular way.
And deeper is the point

Beyond all that practical stuff, sex is extremely important for building and renewing the connection. I also think that if two people aren’t having sex, it becomes hard to explain how they’re different from regular friends. There is a real contradiction here. I don’t think it needs to be solved into a rule.

I think sex is especially important while the bond is forming. It may be what turns a friendship into a romance and keeps feeding the romantic connection. But if the connection gets deep enough, sex appeal stops being the basis of the relationship. You don’t stop loving the person because she got old, he lost his job, one of you got sick, or sex became impossible.
Sometimes they may even want you to find sexual satisfaction elsewhere if they can’t give it, because they love you and want you to be happy. Maybe they don’t. Nobody is owed that as proof of love.
How to find a partner
(Insert OKCupid sponsorship here)

Looking for a partner is arguably backward, and can work against you. You can’t help looking if you want one, but once you start seeing every new person as a potential partner, you perform for them and they perform for you. Try to see people for who they are before you think of them that way. Actually it was Bee who kept drilling this into me: “You see a pretty girl, but you don’t see the ugly stuff she’s dealing with inside.”

On the other hand, if you aren’t looking for one, then you also aren’t filtering & comparing potential matches, which makes you more vulnerable to someone who targets you with their love bombs, not to mention the potentially good matches may slip thru the cracks of indifference.

Maybe a good compromise is to look for people that match you without directly looking for a romantic match. Join a local group that fits your interests. Go forage for wild plants, meditate, hike, study philosophy, whatever. At least you have fun, learn something, and maybe make some friends even if nobody attractive shows up.
Long distance

I don’t think anyone wants to have a long-distance relationship, unless they’re not ready for a real in-person one, or it just so happens that their dream partner is currently far away. There is something super romantic about preferring one person no matter the distance. But it’s also not something we evolved to feel fulfilled by. And the less you’re physically together, the less you actually know each other. And actually, I would find it more romantic for my partner to say, “Let’s be together at any cost, physically” rather than “You should go take that better job and I’ll stay here.”

If you’re just starting one of these, I’d suggest you ask your partner about how long they are comfortable maintaining distance, to see if it really matches what you want. If you’re already in a relationship of any type, it’s worth discussing how much distance you’d tolerate and for how long.
Dating App Horror Show

I would never recommend dating apps based on my own experience, although I suppose it depends on the person. Maybe you don’t care much about spirituality or anything, you’re not unique and don’t care if they are, you just “like big butts and you cannot lie,” and they want the same sort of thing. Then maybe the app fits what you’re looking for. 😅

Case in point, OKCupid didn’t tell me my first wife was going to try to kill me and my family, take my son, and then put me on child support that I can’t pay and wouldn’t pay on principle if I could. That was the worst choice I ever made, even though I still love my son and I’m happy he was born.

On the other hand, the app did give me information that I ignored because she was cute and interested in me. Her OKCupid profile almost made her sound like a prostitute, or at least someone who liked casual sex. Both turned out to be true. But once she started chatting with me and I saw the nice photos, I thought maybe she had been joking in the profile or something.
These days almost nobody even has a profile. They just have photos, which is showing you something too.

Ok wait, Judge not, lest ye be judged... An app could be fine as an introduction if you use it as a proper gate. Assume 99.99% of the people there are a bad match for you. If you’re just going to get excited by every cute guy or girl who hits you up, forget it. That’s such an easy way to find a weirdo, a psycho, a mooch, a faker, or whatever. Those people are easy enough to find in modern society in person anyway.

I always tell young guys especially: don’t worry about not finding a girl. Worry about finding the wrong girl. Girls are usually more selective, but they still need to think twice, because they often go for guys who aren’t respectful or mature.

I’m almost embarrassed to admit, but I recently tried Hinge again for a few days while I was in Kenya after my last breakup. I was getting something like a hundred girls interested in my profile every day, so I looked through a lot of profiles. Some were cute but none seemed deep. So the app did tell me something useful.
Community makes the match

Sometimes when you don’t go looking, others go looking for you! Some time in my teen years, my dad decided I needed a girlfriend. This was long before dating apps, so he suggested we put up posters around the neighborhood advertising me as eligible for girls to date. I was horrified and we dropped the idea. That gives you some idea of the mildly autistic background I’m coming from: we didn’t understand people. That’s why it might seem absurd the level to which I’m trying here to help you understand what perhaps is already obvious. 😅

The advantage of meeting through your community, unlike through an app, is that you see someone over time. Other people know them. You see how they act when they aren’t on a date, what they’re like with friends, and what happens when they’re irritated, bored, jealous, or not getting what they want.
Community also supports you regardless of who your baby daddy may be, and you aren’t desperate for just any kind of closeness because hopefully the community already fulfills most of that need.

But if you don’t have community, the move is to find someone who is also looking for one that would interest you both. You can visit communities together (like Tree & Julia’s YT), or at least make a real plan to eventually live in one together. It’s a wide world, and traveling around looking at possible communities is a supremely good way to get to know someone.
On the other hand, you may end up having sex too fast if you’re traveling together, but I’d still rather have sex with someone who’s trying to find a commune with me than someone I met at a party.
The Missing Middle

Modern life barely has an intermediate stage between being interested in somebody and getting sexually entangled. One old example is bundling, a mostly extinct practice now especially associated with the Amish, even though it existed much more widely. Courting couples could spend the night together in bed, usually clothed, with the idea that they could talk and be close without having sex. It sounds a lot like the missing middle I’m talking about.

It also didn’t exactly solve the problem. In late-eighteenth-century New England, bundling coexisted with a lot of premarital pregnancy: 30–40 percent of brides were already pregnant. So it wasn’t exactly a reliable way to keep courtship nonsexual. I don’t think we need to bring bundling back, but we do need some socially recognized way to explore tenderness and attraction without immediately sliding toward sex, cohabitation, and a life bond.
Starting on the right foot
The window of clarity, and how it closes

For me, the window of objectivity starts closing abruptly once it seems like sex will definitely be happening soon and I’m flowing with that timeline. I begin idealizing her more, and after sex I may suddenly feel unable to leave because maybe she’s pregnant, etc.

Maybe I’m not representative of the modern degen dating scene. If you’re quite numb and used to casual sex, perhaps the window closes later, or even never. But for me, this is the pattern, and it seems like it would be healthy in a healthy, natural, small society.

The attachment theory part isn’t just from my own experience. It comes from reading I’ve done as well. Sex turns on bonding chemistry—oxytocin, dopamine, vasopressin—that usually biases us toward attachment.

People call oxytocin the “love hormone,” as if getting more attached should make you feel closer and safer. If closeness was safe when you were little, maybe it does feel a bit like coming home. But if it came with neglect, abuse, or if people disappeared on you, you can get more attached and more freaked out at the same time. You might get anxious or suspicious. You might feel worthless or fight or flight mode may kick in.

Peeking thru the window

Before the wisdom window closes, the main thing is to find out whether you are actually compatible. Do you have the same goals and values, especially around children, religion, politics, health, love, and romance? Where do you want to live? Do you both want to find a community? What kind of relationship do you want with technology and money?
Ask deep questions. Conversation-card games may seem silly, but they can help people get past superficial talk and see if they’re compatible.

But asking, “How do you handle jealousy?” can get me a beautiful answer that tells me almost nothing. I’d rather ask what she thinks she would do in an actual situation. If all she can give me is a general answer, I assume she probably doesn’t know yet.

A card game can create its own little high too. If we spend two hours telling each other things nobody else knows, we may feel incredibly understood and close. That may mean the game worked without telling us whether the relationship will.

You can also bring the person to a party and see how they act, bring them around your family or friends, or take them to activities you enjoy and see if they really enjoy them too. Try doing what you would normally do in your day alone, but with them, and see how it feels. Is it weird? Are they wondering why you do this stuff? Do they look bored, like they’d rather just hit you up later than be with you while you’re doing ordinary stuff? Can you guys be normal together and not just romantic or dating?

See their negative side first too. If there is no negative side, that’s a red flag for fakery. Ask whether the spiritual story they tell about themselves survives an inconvenient PMS afternoon. How recent is the healing story—two months or two years? Jealousy, abandonment, possessiveness, and the “I’m so much better than I used to be” story may not be understood until there is stress and entanglement. By then, of course, you’re stressed and entangled. 😆

Sometimes the only thing I have is a little “wait” feeling. It doesn’t prove anything. But if I’m about to ignore a question because I really want this to work, that’s enough reason for me to ask the question before I keep going.

If they’re nasty to their friends, family, or other people, assume they will eventually be nasty to you. We mostly seem to get attracted to the inner-child part because we’re coming from our inner child and we want to have fun. But you also need to find out whether there is a healthy adult there before you’re too bonded to want the answer.
The conversation about flaws
Card games and social gatherings don’t tell you everything, but I wouldn’t ask someone out of the blue, “What did you do wrong in your past relationships?” That would be a pretty weird date.

At the right time, though, in the right way (especially if they bring it up tangentially), I would ask about their past relationships, especially the recent ones. If every story ends with everything being the other person’s fault, I’d ask, “Okay, so what lessons did you find for yourself?”
“I have baggage” tells me almost nothing. What are you having trouble with now? What might make it hard for you to function well in a relationship?

I’d want both of us to be honest about how effective we actually are at handling our own issues. What addictions or impulsive behaviors can’t we reliably control? How dependable are we? What are we probably going to ask forgiveness for more than once? That tells me more than either of us announcing that we’re healed.

The most recent conflicts are the best place to look. Were you able to regulate at all during the conflict? What did you do to the other person? How did you repair afterward? What did you learn? Has your judgment gotten better, or do you keep falling for the same stuff?
I’d also want to know what their friends or exes would say, because people aren’t always the best judges of their own progress.
And if somebody tells me, “I shut down,” okay, what does that mean? Did you stop talking to your partner for days? Did they feel abandoned?
My flaws

My own list isn’t especially flattering. I’m impulsive. I idealize too much, although I don’t demonize. I’m very open and not very private. I care more about honesty than the standard romantic ideal. I still love my exes. After being deeply in love, I have overly high expectations, so I’m hard to please with a basic relationship.

I’m also extremely unique and have deeply held convictions many people won’t agree with. I’m anti-vax, anti-money, anti-civilization, etc. And I’m not yet living the way I want to live (astrology predicts I will by 2030 😃).
A woman should know that before she starts fitting me into the life or fantasy she already planned.

Key was an inner-child therapist and Reiki healer. Both Key and Bee were extremely curious and open-minded, which I loved about them. They were open to spiritual experiences, very connected to childlike wonder, and were always seeing what they needed to work on. They both meditated a lot.
I saw all that and thought anyone with that much spiritual depth and curiosity must already be far along on the path.

That was my mistake. Their meditations may have helped them a lot. I still had no idea how either woman would act when a relationship got ugly. If somebody starts with enough trauma, huge progress can still leave a lot unresolved.

My own blind spot is that I have trouble understanding where people are at mentally and emotionally. A partner may agree with everything I say and then tell me later, “Didn’t you understand I was FAWNING?”
No, I really didn’t. If you’re fawning, tell me when you can, because I can’t know what’s happening in your head just because it feels obvious to you.
Things get tricky fast

Couples withdraw from friends who aren’t supportive of the romantic dyad, and they also stop telling friends the whole truth. Sharp questions start to feel rude. An obvious problem dissolves into, “but I love her,” and the small world of the relationship starts feeling more real than the rest of life. The relationship can close off at exactly the point when both people most need a view from outside it.
Sometimes withdrawing isn’t wrong. Telling your friend, “Can you believe what my girlfriend is doing to me?” can be a privacy violation. It’s just important to realize what is happening.

It doesn’t help if she tells her friends her side while I tell mine mine. We need people who actually know both of us over time, well enough that the relationship isn’t the only reality in the room. I’ll come back to that.
Beware idealization in either direction
Idealization can be pathological, but it can also come very close to real deep love and appreciation. That’s why it’s so easy to get confused.

So far in my life the main experiences of this have been with Bee and Key. They’re also the two women I’ve actually been in love with, which is probably not a coincidence. Both of them saw me as their knight in shining armor, and that brought out this divine-feminine beauty in them that made me into a real love slave. I’m not Superman out here trying to “save a hoe.” There’s just a natural director/muse dynamic that sometimes plays out in an exaggerated way.
It shouldn’t have to happen that way, though. It’s a bad shortcut to the divine archetypes.

Legitimately seeing someone as amazing doesn’t depend on what the seeing gives you. Once you start identifying with the way you see them—she’s perfect, this is destiny, I’m the one who finally found her—you’re already lost in the sauce.

The degree of idealization also predicts the degree of demonization for me. I don’t mean this as a clinical diagnosis, but I use it almost diagnostically in my own life. If a woman says, “You’re such a great guy. Of course you have flaws like anyone, but I love you,” that sounds healthy. If she says, “You’re perfect. I can’t find any flaw,” I’m already running.

When the BPD splitting happens, private hatred can replace worship. Then come public accusations, rewriting the whole past and treating every flaw as proof that the person was fake all along. Sometimes the woman who thought I was perfect later accuses me of thinking I’m perfect.

I’ve learned to get nervous when somebody knows too much about me too soon. We’re twin flames. She knows my motives. I’m Lord Krishna. Okay, maybe I really am way better than the other guys she’s found. But if she hasn’t found anything about me that bothers her yet, she hasn’t found all of me.

For example, I still love women I’ve loved before. Sometimes I talk about them because I’m thinking about them. I’m not trying to make her jealous. If she can’t handle that I still love them, she isn’t ready for me.

If she says, “Can you talk less about your exes?” Sure. Maybe I do talk about them too much sometimes. But they still matter to me. If I’m supposed to listen to everything on her mind, I don’t want to have to pretend that isn’t on mine.
Anti-PTSD Can Be Just As Dangerous As PTSD
When I’m in love, I see everything just from the love angle. I should probably admit that before I give anybody more advice.

A friend in my TherapyCircle chat was talking about PTSD recently, and I said, “I have anti-PTSD.” I coined it as a joke, but even though it feels nice to have Anti-PTSD, it can leave me at more risk than if I had PTSD. Instead of expecting danger, I keep expecting each new woman and each new situation to finally be the beautiful exception. I see the good. I give the benefit of the doubt long after it has stopped being a benefit. Then the false positive resolves into the same old pattern and gives me actual PTSD, like Ping Pong.

I grew up assuming the best of everybody because that’s what my parents taught me. Now I’m trying to be more suspicious and check for red flags before I’m alone with somebody I badly want to please. Why does she contact me only sometimes? What’s the pattern? Is she communicating enough for me to really know her interest level and what’s underneath it? Would my twin flame behave like this? That’s my question. Not everybody is searching for somebody who will naturally channel the divine in their presence.

My second marriage to Bee is the clearest example. I knew within a week of her visiting that she saw me as her father. I didn’t know where that might lead, and it seemed like the only avenue to her heart, so I went with it.

That dynamic alone isn’t necessarily the main problem. A lot of women have seen me that way. The question is whether they can hold it lightly, playfully, and curiously, or whether it turns into something all-enveloping, and they start taking everything they feel about their dad out on me as if I’m him. With Bee, the main issues were the BPD and that her aunts had badly witchcrafted her as a child. She would tell you the same.

She loved me openly and intensely and seemed to understand me spiritually. Most of all, there was the forest-and-mansion line I mentioned earlier that made it feel unconditional. Best drug I ever had.

I don’t know whether that unconditional love ended up being true. I think it was true in a part of her, and it may also have been the BPD idealization. You have to look at everything from multiple angles. But when you’re in love, you see everything from the love angle. That’s the reality shift I’m talking about. It’s great if the ground underneath is prepared for it. If the rose-colored glasses go on when you’re with the wrong person, they make it even harder to understand what’s real.

So I became the father in a relationship where I wanted an equal. Part of what happened may have been that she eventually grew up, and a daughter who grows up leaves home. That wasn’t the whole story. The two years in-between contained enough insanity for several lifetimes.

Looking back, I’m grateful I loved her. For three months after we broke up, I trained myself to replace missing her with loving her, and now, any time I think of her, I feel so much joy and love, which I send her way.

text: That doesn’t mean I’d advise somebody to knowingly enter a dangerous relationship because it may be worth it. Going in, it helps to recognize your pattern, stop idealizing without becoming suspicious and closed, and have some idea what you’re getting into.
Seeing idealization right
You can see something in a person before she fully lives it, but then you have to ask her:
“I see this in you, and I think it’s special. Do you wanna reach for it together?”

If she says no, forget it. You’re in la la land. If she says yes, ask what is blocking her. Is the block more than you can handle? Or does she mostly need somebody to join her on the journey and believe in her?

Partners should help each other grow. Who else is going to do it? Your mom and dad? You’re already grown to them. Everybody else will usually be a smaller influence, so you’d better choose someone who helps you grow well. Like the FM Laeti song down in the Twin Flames section says, “Inspire her to see the best in herself, actualize that.” If something severe is happening, sometimes a demand or boundary is necessary too.
If slow isn’t realistic for you

I pretty much always intend to wait long enough to have this conversation and figure out who I’m dealing with. Then the heat of the moment hits and I want her to think of me as the guy who pleases her, not the guy who makes her think twice about wanting pleasure.

So my main strategy has been to avoid heat-of-the-moment situations until I’m ready. That has definitely saved me from having ten times the body count, but it doesn’t work reliably because the request often starts out small. “Hey, wanna go do something together?” Maybe she wants me to come to an event, a meditation teaching, or a walk in nature.

Phone or video first can help. So can meeting around other people and deciding beforehand that we aren’t going home together. Islamic and conservative Christian cultures put much stronger barriers around a man and woman being alone before marriage. I don’t accept their helicoptering solution, but they noticed something real. We don’t live in tribes anymore, where people around us might know both of us well enough to slow this down.
Just in case

We’re human though, so expecting perfect behavior is a recipe for disaster. That’s where Gandarussa comes in for men. It’s a traditonal Indonesian contraceptive herb that looks about 99% effective, with health benefits (including libido and for HIV), and rarely any side effects. You have to take it daily and it takes a month to become effective. That only deals with pregnancy, though. I can still get emotionally attached to somebody I barely know.
Holding up a leaky dam

Once I’m attached, “I’m taking a chance on her” starts turning into “she’s the right person” after we’ve been together for a while. Based on what? Sometimes I actually learned something. Sometimes nothing changed except that now I’m attached, and the new certainty is just harder for me to question.

If I have sex with somebody quickly, that’s a reason not to move in quickly too. Moving in together right away is basically getting into a common-law marriage without discussing it. I want us to keep seeing friends, have some kind of community around the relationship, and pick actual dates to ask how it’s going. Otherwise it’s too easy for me to assume the relationship is going well because we’re already entangled.
I can know I want her much faster than I can know whether I want to raise children with her, live in community with her, or build a life with her.
At some point one of you will ask, “Why am I special to you? Why are you with me and not somebody else?” If the answer is basically, “We had sex and got hitched?” I don’t know, that’s a damn shame.
Slow & steady may win the race, but turtles have problems too!

Going slowly can show you how somebody’s moods move over time, how they treat you, and how they treat other people. It still can’t tell you how good the sex will be or how either of you will act afterward.

You can know somebody for twenty years and then discover on the first night that the polarity isn’t there, touch or smell feels wrong, your desire levels or kinks don’t fit, one person is sexually shut down, or the bodies just don’t connect.
Some of those things might get better if both partners are committed to helping each other through it. Sometimes bad sexual fit still feels like, “Let’s just be friends!”

Saying, “The sex isn’t working for me,” may sound like, “I only love you if the sex is good.” But universal love doesn’t make someone special. It isn’t romance. It’s the basis of any good relationship of any kind.
I can still love her and not want to be in a romantic relationship with her. Romantic love generally needs good sex too, or we’re friends who care deeply about each other.
Slow & steady isn’t KO’d yet

Slow and steady might still apply after the shock of the first night together. At the beginning of my sexual relationship with Bee, she told me, “You’re going to get a lot better at sex.” (God forbid I tell a woman that.) Funny thing is, I don’t think I did. She got much better at receiving me.

About eighteen months later, she could orgasm almost immediately from penetration without foreplay, have dozens of orgasms in 5 minutes, and squirt so much we were flooding the bed. We were often making love for at least four hours a day. The rest of the day was spent doing laundry loads.

After we broke up, I was extremely curious whether that would simply transfer to another man. Last year she told me that in the five years since me, she had tried having sex with somebody else once. It felt so bad that she stopped after about a minute.
So “trainable” doesn’t quite describe what I mean. Some sexual abilities can obviously be trained, but some sexual responsiveness seems to be co-created between particular people.

The strangest part was that Bee’s body kept opening more while consciously she was trusting me less and becoming more sure that she wanted to separate. She used to say, “I can’t stand you! but I LOVE you and I don’t know why!”

Women are always demanding to know why I love them. Apparently they’re allowed not to know. Those double-standards really bug me, but I also understand our brains work differently. So that’s another thing to learn about over time in a relationship, and it sometimes hits you unexpectedly.
So go slowly if you can. Just don’t imagine that means you know everything. You learn what you can before sex. Sex itself tells you other things.
The Relationship As Crucible

It was during my first marriage that I read about Dr. David Schnarch’s Crucible Approach in Passionate Marriage. Schnarch saw marriage as a natural “people-growing process.” His idea of differentiation was learning to hold onto yourself while staying close, especially when intimacy brings anxiety and unresolved problems to the surface.
That’s definitely what relationship has done to me.

One warning before I romanticize the crucible too much: sometimes (as in my first marriage) this isn’t two wounded people triggering each other but one person terrorizing or controlling the other. If you’re scared to say no or tell the truth, or scared of what happens if you leave, don’t treat that as a mutual communication exercise—get other people involved and think about safety first.

Toft sees the crucible of his marriage as his main spiritual practice. He also continues his meditation, yoga, prayer, and church activities, but sees them as secondary. I understand what he means. It’s much easier for me to feel spiritually advanced when nobody is close enough to expose the parts of me that aren’t.

Being in a relationship showed me how vulnerable I actually am when I open my heart. It’s really easy to feel invulnerable and strong when you’re alone, or even just with friends. Taking off the masks and showing your inner child is a gamble, but it’s required if you want to go deeper in yourself and deeper with another person.
From flow to nitty gritty

Living alone is easy in so many ways. I can make my bed whenever I want. When I have a girlfriend, making the bed in the morning can become one of the ways I show her I love her. If I don’t do it well, somehow it may become a bad omen that I don’t care about her.
A tiny thing can end up carrying way more emotional weight than it should.

Dealing with somebody else’s emotional insecurities can also be exhausting. It’s easy to feel free when I don’t have to do that, especially since I’m a bit of an introvert and 10% autistic. All that works wonderfully until I’m in a romantic relationship and suddenly I’m expected to mind-read, notice every emotional shift, check in constantly, and understand what a silence means, without manipulating based on all that expert “management.”
Reverting to babyhood

Relationship may activate wounds that were already there. Sometimes it may open a level of the heart that is simply very young and vulnerable, whether you knew there was a wound there or not. You become like a baby again. There’s a reason lovers call each other “baby.”
That can be an incredible therapy opportunity. Every such opportunity also carries a risk of failure and more trauma.

With Bee, Key, and H., there was always some sense that they were remembering how their dad treated them and judging me according to how close to him—or different from him—I was. That puts me in a tough position. I want to play the role they need in some way, but I don’t want to leave the reality of me being me.
A smaller example happened with all of them. They could message me whenever they wanted, even a day later. If I took a day to respond, suddenly it was weird. What was I doing? What did it mean?
The present issue may be tiny. The part reacting to it may be five years old.
Don’t make your partner your whole world
When I’m in love, my partner is my everything. Everything else drops away. I still try to make some time for friends, but really all I want to do is be with her.

That little paradise is wonderful, but it contains the seed of its own destruction. Part of why it feels like a magical wonderland is that you can suddenly stop parenting yourself now that you have someone who’s fully got your back. This makes you soft and weak, kinda like a sweet treat or heroin. It is wonderful to have their love and support, but don’t let that bring you away from your own self-love, reparenting, meditation, yoga, and other healing practices that keep you independently healthy. Otherwise, you’ll end up blaming them when you feel bad.

So don’t let your world get so small. Don’t abandon your friends unless they really aren’t good for the relationship. And if they aren’t, ask why. Are they bad friends? Are they slyly interested in one of you romantically? Or is the relationship so weak that it can’t handle anybody with an outside view?
You don’t need to spend as much time with friends as you did before the romance. But keep some room to explore life on your own.
For me, that also means keeping close friends, outside therapy when I need it, a mission of my own, separate interests, some connection to community, and the ability to be alone.

Toft also points out that a man can get feminine energy from nature, music, poetry, art, flowers, food, and other parts of life. I like that idea. A girlfriend shouldn’t have to be my only source of beauty, softness, sensuality, and inspiration.
I’d rather make alone time normal than wait until I’m already overwhelmed and suddenly announce, “I need time for myself!” By then it can easily sound like I need time away from her.
And bring each other out into the world. See people together. Go places. Don’t just disappear into each other.
Disconnect to connect
Self-reflection is a good place to start, but it can’t see what it can’t see.
A peer can give another angle. Your partner is also usually trying to keep you, so they have an ulterior motive that a peer counselor hopefully does not.
That’s why I recommend peer counseling outside the couple. If my partner is the only person I bring all my pain to, she also ends up carrying whatever I do when I still don’t understand it.

I also have to deal with what happens in my body. My mind may understand that my partner is going through something difficult and that I don’t have to be dragged down with her. Meanwhile my body feels dragged down, fragile, and sensitive. My breathing gets shallow. It becomes extremely hard to feel okay while she is in pain.

Crying helps a lot, but it may actually be harder for men once they are in a relationship because they are expected to be the shoulder everybody else cries on. That is another reason to have a peer counselor.

Crying also contains a type of automatic erratic breathwork. Breathwork is one of the easiest ways I know to calm down. Reduced breathing or the Buteyko method is especially useful to me when my partner is getting me upset and flustered with drama. Sometimes she’s deliberately trying to do that. Other times it’s hard to tell. I explain more of the body-based options in my Somatic Modalities guide.

Meditation is also helpful. For most people, I would still put inner-child reparenting, peer counseling, and body-based work first or make them primary meditation targets. Many people say they cannot meditate or have not gotten to that stage yet. Meditation without grounding in those approaches can easily be a road into spiritual bypassing.
Babies growing up again

Nobody has to be completely healed before entering a relationship. And I think that as we learn more about ourselves through the crucible, we should naturally raise our standards. Maybe at first we need the drama to access our primal emotions, but after years of that, we’re exhausted by what we previously hoped to find.
At the very least, there needs to be honesty, real effort at improving, and some ability to stop blaming everybody else for your own problems.

I already said before dating that the present-day adult has to be able to parent whatever intimacy wakes up inside you. Once you’re together, more of that stuff comes out. Inner-child reparenting means parenting the child part instead of surreptitiously hiring the partner for the job.

It can get pretty entitled when you expect your partner to know what you need without being told. You may barely see your own pattern, and then deny it instead of taking responsibility when they point it out.
Some babies grow up faster

While different maturity levels are to be expected to some degree, it can get out of hand at the extremes. What I noticed in all of my most intimate relationships was that when one person was always the child and the other is always the therapist, guru, doctor, or dad, then it’s too unequal, and eventually there will be some kind of pendulum swing or backlash. When I became consistently the responsible one, that also made me responsible for everything that went wrong, not to mention the unhealthy clinginess, jealousy, and all the rest which went along with that dynamic.

Toft says, “She’s not a girl,” and “She’s not your mother.” I agree with the warning, but I’d qualify the first sentence. A lot of women enjoy a daddy/little-girl dimension with a man they trust, and I don’t see a reason to deny them that. It can be affectionate, erotic, comforting, or playful.
The problem is when the role takes over the relationship. She can be my little girl sometimes without becoming my child. She still has to remain responsible for her life and keep reparenting herself.
It can run the other way too. If I expect her to regulate me, soothe every wound, organize my life, and keep me functional, then I’ve made her Mom.
All three women told me at some point that they felt like my patient, and I couldn’t exactly argue with them. They asked me about almost every medical, mental-health, and practical problem:
“I’m sick. What should I take?”
“I’m sad. What should I do?”
I usually had some idea, so of course I answered. But enough moments become a pattern.

Key at first asked me innocently, “Can you be my guru?” I told her, “I’m not anyone’s guru, but we can learn from each other.” A few months later, she was telling me she was much more spiritually advanced than me. I asked, “Do you recall asking me to be your guru?” She said, “Wow, I must have been really confused back then!”

I also have to admit, I can become condescending when somebody stops taking responsibility for their behavior. I find that intolerable. If someone says, “I feel like your patient,” both people need to look at their roles.

I know what can happen on my side. Helping feels good. Being needed can feel good too. A lot of the time I really did have the information or perspective they needed, so of course they kept asking me. I also had to look at whether they were trying to take care of themselves without me.
Different levels in different domains can be complementary

According to myself, I was ahead of Bee, Key, and H. in maturity, emotional stability, self-love, and self-awareness. I also had advantages they didn’t, including a happier childhood and more moolah. As you might imagine, all of that affected the balance between us.

They were all ahead of me in childlike wonder and fascinating creative intuition, which is what attracted me. Sometimes their intuition was wrong and they trusted it too much, but I still loved that quality in them, since I tend to be more analytical.

They were also all more social than me. They could organize people for a ceremony or group gathering very easily. I felt like I needed that if I ever wanted to start a commune, because I’m more introverted.

I’m good at talking to people when there’s a purpose. I’m not as good at rousing everybody up and encouraging them to do things or go places with me, because I tend to feel that everyone should simply do as they please.
So I do believe in mutual coaching and complementarity.

I could teach these women about loving and reparenting their inner child, Buddhism, meditation, and other things I understood better. They could pull me into life more, show me where I was missing people, and sometimes be the skeptic when I was seeing the best in someone and missing their hidden motives.
The roles can flip: teacher one day, student the next. That’s healthy.

Once one person has become the default caregiver and that’s taken for granted, it’s time to bring in other support, lest the romance collapse under the burden. Maybe the romance actually does need less intensity, maybe it becomes friendship, or maybe it ends. I can’t answer that for others, and I couldn’t always answer it for myself, but asking the question out loud is usually where it starts.
The next two sections are about masculine–feminine polarity and Twin Flames. If neither is relevant to you, skip ahead to Two Pillars Don’t Hold The Roof Up.
Primal attraction: channeling the Divine Masculine & Feminine

Everything I’ve been putting forward so far has leaned toward honesty, closeness, and equal dignity. I do believe in that basically for any type of relationship, but none of that by itself explains why two people still want to tear each other’s clothes off each night.
For me, safety gives the space for desire, even if it doesn’t spark it.

When I feel safe with a woman, we can actually tell each other our fantasies without worrying that the other is going to be horrified or weaponize it later. We can imagine pregnancy and really enjoy the thought that we might be making a baby, rather than imagining I’m ejaculating into a condom and hoping nothing happens.
Whenever I was scared of getting a woman pregnant, the sex was usually much more boring.

So why is it that a lot of relationship advice says desire needs distance, mystery, withholding, maybe even separate homes? I suspect they are compensating for a lack of expressed difference while together.
The more safety there is, the more closeness there is, the more polarity there needs to be to keep things alive and poppin’.
Some women may only get turned on by pathology and danger. A woman may also feel her man has become so feminine that there is no contrast left.

A lot of women want to feel that the man is dangerous in some way, but preferably in an exciting and defending way rather than threatening. Beauty and the Beast is a “tale as old as time” for a reason.
The real question is whether polarity stays alive inside the safety.
Muses & Directors

In ordinary life, I sometimes think of the woman as the engine and myself as the steering wheel. I get motivation from her. She is the life force. She brings inspiration, beauty, intuition, creativity, and this feeling that life is worth doing.
I help give it direction and make it operational.

I find the intuitive mind incredibly sexy, because I can’t fully follow it. During sex, some of the most “womanly” women I’ve loved have gone through psychic experiences, memories that felt like past lives, and things I had no idea how to explain. One time, Bee said she almost got enlightened, but I came too fast. Woops...

Key could sometimes start talking and somehow teleport me outside the galaxy. I don’t know how else to describe it. Her voice would become so beautiful that I would shed tears that felt super liberating.
Bee could bring out something similar--she could be talking to me for hours on end, but instead of trying to mute her with the TV remote, I felt I was in a timeless dimension of love.
Maybe women are poetry and men are prose.

Some women barely have that poetic quality, and artistic men can live much closer to it. I’m referring more to feminine vs masculine archetypes. What attracts me is the feminine intuitive leap, because it’s hard for me to understand, seems often absurd, yet many times may turn out more accurate than what I could have figured. I hope this feminine quality can be treasured by all girls as they grow, without falling into helplessness or chaos that over-relying on it without calibration could create. Boys should also maintain their access to this, even if it’s not primary.

This polarity is attracting, but it also shows up in arguments. Toft says that after fifty years of marriage, sometimes his wife wants to talk while he wants to fix, a la Men are From Mars, Women are from Venus. I recognize that as well. So I ask, “Do you want me to help figure this out, or do you mostly want me to listen?” Listening doesn’t mean I’m gonna be a doormat tho. If I start listening to her demonize me, that’s the Crucible safety problem I already talked about.

Where I like the polarity is when she sees the Big Picture, and I help fill in the details to make our plan workable. If she micromanages, I start feeling useless. If she earns more than me, although that’s not inherently problematic, it often becomes so, because she will naturally start to feel like she is the one who should make the decisions (”My house, my rules”).

She may know much more than I do about some particular field, including a traditionally non-feminine one, and in that case I want her help. “Honey, let me help you with this,” can be very sexy, until helping turns into doing everything for me and I start feeling useless.
In my experience, women often prefer me to say directly:
“This is where I want to go. This is what I think we should do. Are you game?”
She might have a better idea, or just not want to do it, but she still wants me to take initiative.

I don’t think equality means dividing every role 50/50. If I like driving and she likes cooking, great. If she’s way better at something, she’ll probably do more of it. When I’m leading, I still want to know what she sees. Mandar obedeciendo—Lead by following—as the Zapatistas say.
Desire is expressed differently for men & women
Women often show wanting directly. They ask, reach, name what they want, and ask the man to do things for them, even when they could do it themselves.

Men tend to show their wanting through providing, fixing, heavy labor, or trying to become indispensable. Not because men are less needy, but their neediness partly consists of being needed. Emotionally, women express their needs more, but this also allows them to get supported more often and by a wider social net. Men, on the other hand, tend to keep their needs to themselves or put them all onto their woman, especially when it comes to the need for a confidant.

That’s fine, and I am not trying to rock their boat. They might be the people who suggest that you should marry your best friend (or “soul mate” in the TF lingo). Then there are the folks who are deep in the TF theory, believing there is literally one person on Earth who is made for you. I’m also not trying to rock their boat. But I do want to tell my story.
I used to fall into the former camp, then into the latter camp, and now that I’ve experienced two twin flame relationships, I’ve jumped into a new camp I never knew existed.
What two Twin Flames taught me

I used to think there was absolutely no way I could ever fall deeply in love with another woman after my 2nd wife, Bee. No other woman ever connected to me on such a deeply spiritual and deeply feminine level. I always said, “Bee is the ultimate woman in every sense.” But I also suspected I felt that way because of what I conceived a woman should be, and because of the shape of my own inner being.
